title: Unit 1 quiz: Introduction to Version Control

questions.q: What is a version control system?
options: Software that records changes to files over time so you can recall earlier versions
A website for storing photos and videos
A tool that compiles C programs faster
An antivirus that protects your source code
questions.explain: A VCS records what changed, who changed it, when and why, and lets you bring back any earlier version.

questions.q: Which type of version control has a single point of failure?
questions.explain: In a centralized VCS (like SVN) everyone depends on one server. If it is down, nobody can commit or see history.

questions.q: Git is an example of which kind of version control?
questions.explain: Git is distributed: every clone contains the full history, so you can work offline and any copy can restore the others.

questions.q: Which statement about Git and GitHub is correct?
options: Git and GitHub are two names for the same thing
Git is a tool on your computer; GitHub is a website that hosts Git repositories
Git needs the internet to save a commit
questions.explain: Git is the version control tool (works offline). GitHub is a hosting service for Git repositories with team features.

questions.q: Which are benefits of using Git and GitHub? (Choose all that apply.)
options: Full history of who changed what and when
Your code is backed up on GitHub
Your code automatically has no bugs
questions.explain: History, branching and backup are real benefits. Git does not find or fix bugs for you, though its history helps you find when a bug appeared.
Linus Torvalds created Git in 2005 to manage development of the Linux kernel. GitHub was founded later, in 2008.

questions.q: Which command sets your name for every repository on this computer?
questions.explain: --global saves the setting in ~/.gitconfig, used by all your repositories. Without --global (inside a repo) it applies to that repository only.

questions.q: Krish has run the two config commands shown in the lesson. What does this print?
questions.explain: git config <name> without a value reads the setting and prints it.

questions.q: You want a quick summary of the options for git commit inside the terminal. What do you type?
questions.explain: git <command> -h prints a short usage summary. git help commit (or git commit --help) opens the full manual page.

questions.q: In the Git for Windows installer, what should you choose for the initial branch name?
options: It does not matter, you can never change it
questions.explain: GitHub uses main, so overriding the default to main keeps your local and GitHub branches consistent. (It can be renamed later with git branch -m.)

questions.q: Which are good practices when creating your GitHub account? (Choose all that apply.)
options: Use the same email as in git config
Pick a professional username like krish-patel
Turn on two-factor authentication and save recovery codes
Share your password with your team lead so they can push for you
questions.explain: Never share your password. Teammates get access as collaborators on a repository instead.

questions.q: Put the first-time setup steps in order.
items: Download and install Git for Windows
Open Git Bash and run git --version
Set user.name and user.email with git config --global
Create a GitHub account with the same email
questions.explain: Install, verify, configure your identity, then create the GitHub account (same email) and secure it with 2FA.
